analysis.one_liner: Boosts Social Security benefits and pays for it by phasing payroll taxes onto income above the wage cap.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 11, 2025 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing or vote scheduled; one Democratic cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise monthly Social Security checks for retirees, disabled workers, and survivors, with the biggest raises going to people with lower lifetime earnings, and it would switch annual cost-of-living increases to a new inflation index built for seniors' spending. To pay for it, income above the Social Security wage cap (about $176,000 a year) would start being taxed in 2026, with all of it covered by 2030. High earners would get only a small extra benefit for those added taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries — retirees, disabled workers, and survivors. The benefit formula changes lift checks most for lower earners, current beneficiaries get an immediate recomputed (higher) benefit in January 2026, and everyone's annual increase would be tied to an index reflecting what retirees actually buy. The new revenue also strengthens the program's finances.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Raises the replacement factor for the lowest bracket of lifetime earnings from 90 percent to 95 percent, which increases monthly benefits and helps lower earners most.

Raises the second bend point in the benefit formula to $6,300 for 2026 and grows it by an additional percentage point each year starting in 2031, reaching 15 percent higher by 2045; current beneficiaries get their benefits recomputed upward in January 2026 using the same change.

Switches annual cost-of-living adjustments to a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics would build to reflect the spending patterns of people at retirement age — an index that typically runs slightly higher than the general index used today.
Phases in Social Security payroll taxation of earnings above the annual wage cap starting in 2026, with all above-cap earnings covered by 2030, adding revenue to the trust funds that pay benefits.

analysis.who_pays: High earners — workers and self-employed people with income above the annual wage cap — and their employers, who would both pay Social Security tax on the above-cap slice of wages, ramping up through 2030. High earners would receive only a modest benefit credit (a 5 percent factor on above-cap earnings) in return.

drawbacks.text: High earners and their employers would face a new payroll tax on every dollar above the cap, and high earners would earn benefit credit on only a small share of it — a 5 percent factor, far less generous than the 15 percent top factor in the current formula.

The benefit increases and the new elderly price index both raise federal outlays, so the bill's long-term effect on Social Security's finances depends on whether the new tax revenue outpaces the added costs — something the bill text does not itself demonstrate.

The elderly consumer price index does not exist in usable form today; the bill directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to build it, and the size of future cost-of-living increases would hinge on how that index is constructed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a straightforward trade: a meaningful benefit increase weighted toward lower-income seniors, funded by a tax on the top slice of earnings. The main honest objections are that high earners pay in without proportionate benefit credit, and that the added benefit costs must be weighed against the new revenue to know the net effect on solvency. The elderly price index is a reasonable way to index senior benefits but is not yet built.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it; Congress is still in session through early January 2027.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill on December 11, 2025; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
One Senate Democrat cosponsored the bill; no Republicans appear among its supporters.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote after the committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved: beneficiaries' checks are unchanged and high earners keep the current wage cap. The bill's fate sits with the Republican-controlled Senate Finance Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over Social Security and payroll tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has scheduled no hearing or markup on it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor are both Democrats, with no Republican support on the bill so far, and the bill now sits in a Republican-controlled committee; there is no recorded opposition vote yet because it has not reached one.

industries.industry: High earners (wages or self-employment income above the annual cap)
industries.note: They would begin paying Social Security tax on income above roughly $176,000 a year, ramping up through 2030, in exchange for only a small 5 percent benefit factor on those earnings. Their added taxes are the funding source for everyone else's benefit increase.
The bill extends the taxable wage base above the cap, which includes the employer's matching share of the payroll tax, raising labor costs for businesses with highly paid staff.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, one cosponsor, and referral to a Republican-controlled Finance Committee with no action scheduled, the most likely path is that the bill sits in committee for the rest of the Congress, as most Social Security expansion proposals do. Its main near-term role is as a marker in the broader debate over Social Security solvency and benefit levels.
